original.title: Wojapi (Plains Berry Sauce)
original.description: A thick, naturally sweet berry sauce made by the Lakota and other Plains nations, traditionally from chokecherries and served warm with fry bread.
ingredients: 4 cups mixed berries, fresh or frozen (blueberries, blackberries, chokecherries, or juneberries)
2 to 4 tbsp honey or maple syrup, to taste
steps: Combine the berries and 1 cup water in a medium saucepan.
Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a simmer.
Cook for 15–20 minutes, mashing the berries with a potato masher or wooden spoon as they soften.
Stir in honey or maple syrup to taste.
For a thicker sauce, stir the cornstarch into the cold water and whisk it into the simmering berries; cook 2 minutes more until glossy.
Serve warm with fry bread or bannock, or chill and use as a spread.

original.title: Bannock
original.description: A simple skillet bread baked across Canada by First Nations and Métis families, made from pantry staples and cooked over a campfire or stovetop.
ingredients: 1/4 cup lard, butter, or vegetable shortening, cut into pieces
1 tbsp vegetable oil, for the pan
steps: Whisk together the flour, baking powder, salt, and sugar in a large bowl.
Rub the lard into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs.
Pour in the water and stir just until a soft dough forms; do not overmix.
Turn the dough out onto a floured surface and pat it into a round about 1 inch thick.
Heat the oil in a 10-inch cast-iron skillet over medium-low heat.
Place the dough in the skillet, cover, and cook for 10–12 minutes until the bottom is golden.
Flip the bannock and cook, covered, for another 10–12 minutes until it sounds hollow when tapped.
Cut into wedges and serve warm with butter, jam, or wojapi.

original.title: Blue Corn Mush
original.description: A creamy, lavender-gray porridge of finely ground blue cornmeal, a staple breakfast of the Hopi and Diné (Navajo) peoples of the Southwest.
ingredients: 1 tsp culinary ash (juniper ash), optional, to deepen the blue color
steps: Stir the blue cornmeal into 1 cup of cold water to make a smooth paste.
Bring the remaining 3 cups of water and the salt to a boil in a saucepan.
If using, dissolve the juniper ash in 2 tablespoons of hot water and strain it into the pot.
Slowly whisk in the cornmeal paste, stirring constantly to prevent lumps.
Reduce the heat to low and cook, stirring often, for 10–15 minutes until thick and smooth.
Serve hot, drizzled with honey or maple syrup if you like.

original.title: Navajo Mutton Stew
original.description: A hearty stew of bone-in mutton or lamb with potatoes, corn, and green chile, a centerpiece of Diné (Navajo) home cooking, usually served with fry bread.
ingredients: 2 1/2 lb bone-in lamb or mutton shoulder or neck, cut into 2-inch pieces
4 medium potatoes, peeled and cut into chunks
2 cups corn kernels, fresh or frozen
steps: Place the lamb in a large pot with the water and salt and bring to a boil, skimming the foam from the surface.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 1 1/4 hours until the meat is tender.
Add the onion, potatoes, carrots, and celery and simmer for 25 minutes.
Stir in the corn and green chiles and simmer 10 minutes more until all the vegetables are tender.
Season with pepper and more salt to taste.
Serve hot in deep bowls with fry bread on the side.

original.title: Cherokee Bean Bread
original.description: Tender cornmeal dumplings studded with brown beans, wrapped in corn husks and boiled—a traditional Cherokee dish from the Southeast.
ingredients: 2 cups cooked pinto or brown beans, drained, with 1 cup cooking liquid reserved
16 dried corn husks, soaked in hot water for 30 minutes
steps: Bring a large pot of water to a boil.
Mix the cornmeal, baking soda, and salt in a large bowl.
Stir in the boiling water and enough of the hot bean liquid to make a stiff dough that holds together.
Gently fold in the beans so they stay mostly whole.
Divide the dough into 8 portions and shape each into a flat oblong cake.
Wrap each cake in two overlapping corn husks, fold in the ends, and tie with twine.
Drop the bundles into the boiling water, reduce to a steady simmer, and cook for 1 hour.
Drain, cool for a few minutes, and unwrap; serve warm with butter or alongside greens.

original.title: Maple-Roasted Winter Squash
original.description: Winter squash roasted with maple syrup and a pinch of salt, honoring the maple sugaring traditions of the Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe peoples.
ingredients: 1 butternut or 2 acorn squash (about 3 lb total)
3 tbsp melted butter or sunflower oil
2 tbsp toasted sunflower or pumpkin seeds
steps: Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Halve the squash, scoop out the seeds, and cut it into 1-inch slices or chunks (peel butternut; acorn skin can stay on).
Toss the squash with the butter, maple syrup, salt, and pepper on a rimmed baking sheet.
Spread it in a single layer and roast for 35–45 minutes, turning once, until tender and caramelized at the edges.
Sprinkle with toasted seeds and serve warm.

original.title: Ojibwe Wild Rice Soup
original.description: A hearty soup of hand-harvested manoomin (wild rice), the sacred grain of the Ojibwe/Anishinaabe of the Great Lakes, simmered with vegetables and venison or chicken.
ingredients: 6 cups venison, turkey, or chicken broth
2 cups cooked shredded venison, turkey, or chicken
steps: Combine the wild rice and water in a saucepan, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer for 45 minutes until the grains split open; drain any excess water.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the onion, carrots, and celery and cook for 8 minutes until softened.
Add the mushrooms and cook 5 minutes more.
Pour in the broth, add the sage, salt, and pepper, and simmer for 15 minutes.
Stir in the cooked wild rice and shredded meat and simmer 10 minutes to blend the flavors.
Garnish with parsley and serve hot.

original.title: Wild Rice with Cranberries and Hazelnuts
original.description: Nutty Great Lakes wild rice tossed with dried cranberries, toasted hazelnuts, and green onions, a festive side drawing on Anishinaabe foods.
steps: Bring the wild rice, water, and salt to a boil in a saucepan.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 45–50 minutes until the grains are tender and many have split; drain well.
While still warm, toss the rice with the oil and dried cranberries so the berries plump.
Whisk the maple syrup and vinegar together and pour over the rice.
Fold in the hazelnuts and green onions and season with pepper and more salt to taste.
Serve warm or at room temperature.

original.title: Pemmican-Style Energy Bites
original.description: A modern take on pemmican, the dried meat, fat, and berry trail food of the Cree and Plains nations, shaped into easy bites for hiking or travel.
ingredients: 8 oz beef or bison jerky, unseasoned or lightly salted
1/2 cup dried blueberries, cranberries, or saskatoon berries
1/2 cup rendered beef tallow or bison fat, melted
steps: Tear the jerky into pieces and pulse in a food processor until it becomes a fine, fluffy powder.
Add the dried berries and pulse a few times until they are coarsely chopped.
Transfer to a bowl, add the salt, and pour in the warm melted tallow.
Mix thoroughly until the mixture holds together when pressed.
Press firmly into a parchment-lined 8-inch pan or shape into 24 small balls.
Refrigerate until firm, about 1 hour, then cut into bars if using a pan.
Store wrapped in a cool place or the refrigerator for several weeks.

original.title: Sumac Lemonade
original.description: A tart, rosy cold drink steeped from the red berry clusters of staghorn sumac, long enjoyed by Eastern Woodlands peoples in late summer.
ingredients: 6 large clusters ripe staghorn sumac berries (red, not white)
1/4 cup maple syrup or honey, or to taste
steps: Shake the sumac clusters to remove any insects or debris; do not rinse, as that washes away the tart coating.
Place the clusters in a large pitcher or bowl and cover with the cold water.
Gently rub and crush the berries with your hands to release their flavor.
Let steep at room temperature for 1–2 hours until the water is pink and tart.
Strain through a fine sieve lined with cheesecloth or a coffee filter to remove hairs.
Sweeten with maple syrup or honey and serve over ice.

original.title: Navajo Tacos
original.description: Golden fry bread piled high with seasoned beans and beef, lettuce, tomato, and cheese—a beloved powwow and fair favorite throughout Indian Country.
ingredients: 1 can (15 oz) pinto beans, drained, or 1 1/2 cups cooked
1/2 cup chopped roasted green chile or salsa
steps: Brown the ground beef with the onion in a skillet over medium-high heat for 8 minutes, breaking it up as it cooks; drain the fat.
Stir in the chili powder, cumin, and salt and cook for 1 minute.
Add the beans and water and simmer for 10 minutes until thickened, mashing a few beans to make it saucy.
Place a warm fry bread round on each plate.
Spoon the beef and bean mixture over the fry bread.
Top with lettuce, tomatoes, cheese, green chile, and sour cream and serve immediately.

original.title: Haudenosaunee White Corn Soup
original.description: A traditional Iroquois soup of hulled white corn simmered with kidney beans and salt pork or smoked meat, served at gatherings and ceremonies.
ingredients: 2 lb dried hulled white corn (Iroquois white corn or prepared hominy), or 3 cans (29 oz each) white hominy
1 lb salt pork or smoked pork hocks
2 cans (15 oz each) red kidney beans, drained, or 3 cups cooked
steps: If using dried white corn, soak it overnight in plenty of cold water and drain.
Place the corn and pork in a large pot with the water and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat and simmer, partially covered, for 2 1/2 hours until the corn kernels are tender and swollen (30 minutes if using canned hominy).
Remove the pork, pull or dice the meat, and return it to the pot, discarding bone and rind.
Add the kidney beans and turnip and simmer 30 minutes more.
Season with salt and pepper and serve hot.

original.title: Plains Bison Stew
original.description: A rich stew of bison simmered with root vegetables and wild onion flavors, honoring the animal at the heart of Lakota, Blackfoot, and other Plains cultures.
ingredients: 2 lb bison stew meat, cut into 1 1/2-inch cubes
steps: Season the bison with salt and pepper and toss with the flour.
Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the meat in batches, 3–4 minutes per batch; set aside.
Add the onion and garlic and cook for 5 minutes, scraping up the browned bits.
Return the bison to the pot with the broth, bay leaves, and sage and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer gently for 1 1/2 hours; bison is lean, so keep it at a bare simmer.
Add the potatoes, carrots, and rutabaga and simmer 30 minutes more.
Stir in the corn and cook 10 minutes until all the vegetables are tender.
Remove the bay leaves, adjust the seasoning, and serve with bannock or fry bread.

original.title: Pueblo Red Chile Posole
original.description: A deeply flavored stew of hominy and pork in New Mexico red chile, served on Pueblo feast days and throughout the Rio Grande valley in winter.
ingredients: 1 lb dried posole (nixtamal corn), or 2 cans (29 oz each) white hominy, drained
2 lb pork shoulder, cut into 1-inch cubes
1/2 cup ground New Mexico red chile powder (mild or medium)
steps: If using dried posole, rinse it and soak overnight in cold water, then drain.
Put the posole in a large pot with the water and simmer for 2 hours until the kernels burst open (skip this if using canned hominy).
Add the pork, onion, garlic, and oregano and simmer for 1 hour until the pork is tender.
Whisk the red chile powder with 1 cup of the hot broth to make a smooth paste and stir it into the pot.
Season with salt and simmer 20 minutes more to mellow the chile.
Serve hot in bowls, with warm tortillas or oven bread.

original.title: Blue Corn Pancakes
original.description: Light, nutty pancakes made with Southwestern blue cornmeal, a cornerstone grain of the Pueblo, Hopi, and Diné peoples.
ingredients: 3 tbsp melted butter, plus more for the griddle
steps: Whisk together the blue cornmeal, flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and sugar in a large bowl.
In another bowl, whisk the buttermilk, eggs, and melted butter.
Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and stir just until combined; let rest 5 minutes.
Heat a griddle or skillet over medium heat and brush it with butter.
Pour 1/4 cup batter per pancake and cook until bubbles form on top and the edges look set, about 2 minutes.
Flip and cook 1–2 minutes more until cooked through.
Serve warm with maple syrup, honey, or wojapi.

original.title: Kneel-Down Bread
original.description: Fresh sweet corn ground into a moist batter, wrapped in its own husks, and baked—named by the Diné (Navajo) for kneeling to grind corn on a metate.
ingredients: 8 ears fresh sweet corn in husks
steps: Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C) or prepare a bed of hot coals.
Carefully remove the husks from the corn, keeping the large inner husks whole, and set them aside.
Cut the kernels from the cobs and scrape the cobs with the back of the knife to collect the milk.
Grind the kernels in a food processor or meat grinder to a thick, wet batter, then stir in the salt and sugar.
Overlap two husks, spoon 1/3 cup of batter into the center, and fold the husks around it into a packet; tie with a strip of husk.
Arrange the packets seam side down in a baking dish.
Bake for 60–75 minutes until firm, or bury in hot coals and ashes for about 1 hour.
Let cool slightly, then unwrap and serve warm.

original.title: Johnnycakes
original.description: Crisp cornmeal griddle cakes descended from the Narragansett and Wampanoag nokehick, the parched-corn cakes shared with early New England settlers.
ingredients: 2 tbsp butter or bacon fat, for the griddle
steps: Stir the cornmeal, salt, and sugar together in a bowl.
Pour in the boiling water, stirring constantly, until the cornmeal is fully moistened.
Let the batter rest for 5 minutes, then thin with enough milk to make a thick, spoonable batter.
Heat the butter on a griddle or cast-iron skillet over medium heat.
Drop the batter by heaping tablespoons and flatten slightly into 3-inch cakes.
Cook without moving for 5–6 minutes until a golden crust forms, then flip and cook another 5 minutes.
Serve hot with butter and maple syrup.

original.title: Sagamité (Maple Hominy Porridge)
original.description: A Great Lakes porridge of cracked hominy or cornmeal sweetened with maple sugar and enriched with sunflower seeds, eaten for centuries by Algonquian and Haudenosaunee peoples.
ingredients: 1 cup coarse hominy grits or stone-ground cornmeal
1/4 cup maple syrup or 3 tbsp maple sugar
steps: Bring the water and salt to a boil in a heavy saucepan.
Slowly whisk in the hominy grits or cornmeal.
Reduce the heat to low and cook, stirring often, for 20–25 minutes until thick and tender.
Stir in the maple syrup and dried berries and cook 3 minutes more.
Spoon into bowls and top with sunflower seeds.

original.title: Roasted Pumpkin Seeds
original.description: Crunchy, salted pumpkin seeds roasted until golden, a snack enjoyed for generations wherever pumpkins and squash were grown in the Americas.
ingredients: 2 cups raw pumpkin seeds, rinsed and dried
1 tbsp sunflower oil or melted butter
steps: Preheat the oven to 325°F (165°C).
Pick any strings of pumpkin flesh off the seeds and pat them thoroughly dry with a towel.
Toss the seeds with the oil, salt, and chili powder.
Spread them in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet.
Roast for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 8 minutes, until golden and crisp.
Cool completely on the pan before serving.

original.title: Wampanoag Cranberry Sauce
original.description: Cranberries, called sasumuneash by the Wampanoag, simmered with maple syrup into a tart-sweet sauce—a native fruit long used for food and medicine in New England.
steps: Combine the maple syrup, water, orange peel, and salt in a saucepan and bring to a boil.
Add the cranberries and return to a boil.
Reduce the heat and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until most of the berries have burst.
Remove the orange peel and let the sauce cool; it will thicken as it stands.
Serve at room temperature or chilled.

original.title: Cherokee Grape Dumplings
original.description: Soft dumplings simmered in sweet, purple grape juice, a beloved Cherokee dessert traditionally made with wild possum grapes.
ingredients: 4 cups unsweetened Concord grape juice, divided
1/2 cup cold grape juice (taken from the 4 cups)
steps: Combine 3 1/2 cups of the grape juice with the sugar in a wide pot and bring to a boil.
Meanwhile, whisk the flour, baking powder, and salt in a bowl and cut in the butter until crumbly.
Stir in the reserved 1/2 cup grape juice to form a stiff dough.
Roll the dough out on a floured surface to 1/4 inch thick and cut into 1-by-2-inch strips.
Drop the dumplings one at a time into the boiling juice.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 12–15 minutes until the dumplings are cooked through and the juice has thickened.
Serve warm, with a spoonful of cream if you like.

original.title: Choctaw Banaha
original.description: Corn shuck bread from the Choctaw of Mississippi and Oklahoma: a cornmeal dough mixed with field peas, wrapped in husks, and boiled.
ingredients: 1 cup cooked field peas or black-eyed peas, drained
16 dried corn husks, soaked in hot water for 30 minutes
steps: Bring a large pot of water to a boil.
Mix the cornmeal, baking soda, and salt in a bowl.
Pour in the boiling water and stir to make a stiff dough.
Fold in the cooked peas.
Shape the dough into 8 oblong rolls about 4 inches long.
Wrap each roll in two corn husks and tie the ends with thin strips of husk.
Drop the bundles into the boiling water and simmer for 40–45 minutes until firm.
Drain, unwrap, and serve warm with butter or alongside pork and greens.

original.title: Pueblo Green Chile Stew
original.description: A soul-warming stew of roasted green chile, pork, and potatoes, cooked in kitchens across the New Mexico Pueblos every fall chile harvest.
ingredients: 2 lb pork shoulder, cut into 1-inch cubes
2 cups roasted, peeled, and chopped green chiles (mild or hot)
steps: Season the pork with the salt.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat and brown the pork in batches; set aside.
Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes, then add the garlic and cook 1 minute.
Return the pork to the pot with the broth, cumin, and oregano and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 45 minutes.
Add the green chiles and potatoes and simmer, uncovered, for 30 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Taste for salt and serve with warm tortillas or oven bread.

original.title: Pueblo Oven Bread
original.description: A slightly sweet, beehive-oven style yeast bread baked by Pueblo families in outdoor adobe hornos, adapted here for a home oven.
ingredients: 2 tbsp lard or vegetable shortening, melted
steps: Dissolve the yeast in 1/4 cup warm water and let stand for 10 minutes until foamy.
In a large bowl, combine the melted lard, honey, salt, and 1 3/4 cups warm water.
Add the yeast mixture, then stir in the flour a cup at a time to make a stiff dough.
Knead on a floured surface for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise for 1 1/2 hours until doubled.
Punch down, divide in half, and shape each half into a round loaf; for the traditional 'paw' shape, cut a deep slash partway into one side and spread the sections.
Place on greased baking sheets, cover, and let rise 30 minutes.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 40–45 minutes until golden brown and hollow-sounding when tapped.
Cool on racks before slicing.

original.title: Venison Jerky
original.description: Thin strips of venison seasoned and slowly dried, a preservation method practiced by Indigenous hunters across North America for millennia.
ingredients: 2 lb lean venison roast, trimmed of all fat
1 tbsp maple syrup or brown sugar (optional)
steps: Freeze the venison for 1 hour so it is firm and easier to slice.
Cut the meat with the grain into strips 1/4 inch thick.
Mix the salt, pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, maple syrup, and water and toss the strips to coat.
Cover and refrigerate for 6 hours or overnight.
Preheat the oven to 175°F (80°C) and set wire racks over foil-lined baking sheets.
Pat the strips dry and lay them in a single layer on the racks without touching.
Dry in the oven with the door propped open slightly for 4–5 hours, until the jerky bends and cracks but does not snap.
Cool completely and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.

original.title: Sautéed Fiddleheads
original.description: Tender coiled ostrich-fern shoots, a spring delicacy gathered by the Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet) and Mi'kmaq of the Maritimes and Maine, sautéed with wild garlic.
ingredients: 1 tbsp salt, for the cooking water
2 cloves garlic or 4 ramps, thinly sliced
1 tsp lemon juice or apple cider vinegar
steps: Trim the brown ends from the fiddleheads and rub off any papery brown scales.
Wash them in several changes of cold water.
Boil in salted water for 10–12 minutes until tender (fiddleheads should always be fully cooked), then drain.
Melt the butter in a skillet over medium heat and sauté the garlic or ramps for 1 minute.
Add the fiddleheads and cook for 3–4 minutes, tossing, until lightly browned.
Season with salt, pepper, and lemon juice and serve hot.

original.title: Wampanoag Clambake in a Pot
original.description: The coastal New England appanaug, a feast of shellfish, corn, and potatoes steamed over seaweed, adapted to a large stockpot.
ingredients: 1 lb smoked sausage or linguiça, cut into chunks (optional)
4 lb littleneck or steamer clams, scrubbed
2 large handfuls of rinsed rockweed seaweed (optional)
steps: Place the potatoes, onions, and sausage in the bottom of a very large stockpot with the water.
Cover with the seaweed, if using, which adds steam and ocean flavor.
Bring to a boil over high heat, cover tightly, and steam for 15 minutes.
Add the corn on top, cover, and steam 5 minutes more.
Add the clams and mussels, cover, and steam for 8–10 minutes until the shells open; discard any that stay closed.
Lift everything onto a large platter or newspaper-covered table.
Serve with melted butter, lemon wedges, and the pot broth for dipping.

original.title: Akutaq (Yup'ik Berry Whip)
original.description: A whipped Alaskan dessert of fat and wild berries made by Yup'ik and Iñupiat families; this home version uses vegetable shortening, a common modern substitute.
ingredients: 1 cup vegetable shortening (or rendered caribou or moose fat, traditionally)
1/4 cup cold water or seal oil
3 cups mixed berries (cloudberries, salmonberries, blueberries, or cranberries)
steps: Place the shortening in a large bowl.
Beat by hand or with a mixer, adding the cold water a little at a time, until light, white, and fluffy, about 5 minutes.
Beat in the sugar until dissolved.
Gently fold in the berries until evenly mixed.
Spoon into a serving bowl and chill for 30 minutes before serving.

original.title: Stuffed Squash Blossoms
original.description: Delicate squash blossoms filled with a corn and cheese mixture and pan-fried, celebrating a summer harvest prized by the Pueblo peoples and Indigenous farmers across the Southwest.
ingredients: 1/2 cup crumbled fresh cheese or ricotta
steps: Gently open each blossom, pinch out the stamen, and check for insects.
Mix the corn, cheese, green chile, and salt.
Spoon about 1 tablespoon of filling into each blossom and twist the petal tips to close.
Dip each blossom in beaten egg and roll in cornmeal.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium heat.
Fry the blossoms for 2 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Drain on paper towels and serve warm.

original.title: Hidatsa Stuffed Pumpkin
original.description: A whole sugar pumpkin baked with a filling of bison, wild rice, and sunflower seeds, inspired by the Hidatsa and Mandan gardeners of the upper Missouri River.
ingredients: 2 tbsp chopped fresh sage or 2 tsp dried
steps: Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Cut a lid from the top of the pumpkin, scoop out the seeds and strings, and sprinkle the inside with 1/2 tsp salt.
Brown the bison with the onion in a skillet over medium-high heat for 8 minutes; add the garlic for the last minute and drain the fat.
Stir in the wild rice, sunflower seeds, sage, pepper, and remaining salt, and let cool slightly.
Mix in the eggs to bind the stuffing.
Pack the stuffing into the pumpkin, replace the lid, and set it in a baking dish with 1/2 inch of water.
Bake for 1 1/2 hours, until the pumpkin flesh is tender when pierced.
Cut into wedges, serving some pumpkin and stuffing with each slice.

original.title: Rose Hip Tea
original.description: A tangy, vitamin-rich tea from wild rose hips, gathered after the first frost and steeped by many Indigenous nations across the north for winter wellness.
ingredients: 1/2 cup dried rose hips, lightly crushed, or 1 cup fresh rose hips, halved and seeded
1 to 2 tbsp honey or maple syrup (optional)
steps: Place the rose hips and water in a saucepan.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for 10–15 minutes.
Remove from the heat and steep for 5 minutes more.
Strain through a fine sieve lined with cheesecloth to remove the fine hairs.
Sweeten with honey or maple syrup if desired and serve hot.

original.title: Maple Sugar on Snow
original.description: Hot maple syrup boiled to the soft-ball stage and poured over clean snow to make chewy taffy, a sugaring-season treat from the Anishinaabe and Haudenosaunee maple camps.
ingredients: 6 cups packed clean snow or finely shaved ice
steps: Pack the snow firmly into a large shallow pan and keep it in the freezer or outside until needed.
Heat the maple syrup and butter in a heavy saucepan over medium heat.
Boil without stirring until the syrup reaches 235°F (113°C) on a candy thermometer, about 10–15 minutes.
Remove from the heat and let stand 1 minute.
Drizzle the hot syrup in thin lines over the snow.
After a few seconds, roll each strand up onto a fork or popsicle stick and eat right away.

original.title: Cornmeal-Crusted Walleye
original.description: Freshly caught walleye fillets dredged in cornmeal and pan-fried, a lake-country favorite among the Ojibwe and other Great Lakes nations.
steps: Soak the walleye fillets in the milk for 10 minutes.
Mix the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, and paprika in a shallow dish.
Lift each fillet from the milk, let the excess drip off, and press it into the cornmeal mixture to coat both sides.
Heat the oil in a large cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Fry the fillets for 3–4 minutes per side until golden and the fish flakes easily.
Drain briefly on paper towels and serve with lemon wedges and wild rice.

original.title: Eastern Woodlands Venison Stew
original.description: Venison slowly simmered with corn, beans, squash, and wild herbs, reflecting the hunting and farming traditions of the Eastern Woodlands nations.
ingredients: 2 lb venison shoulder, cut into 1 1/2-inch cubes
1 1/2 cups cooked kidney or cranberry beans
steps: Season the venison with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the meat in batches; set aside.
Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes until softened.
Return the venison to the pot with the broth, sage, and thyme and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer gently for 1 3/4 hours until the venison is tender.
Add the squash and simmer for 20 minutes.
Stir in the beans, corn, and maple syrup and simmer 10 minutes more.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot.

original.title: Sofkee
original.description: A mildly sour, thin corn drink of the Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole peoples, made from cracked hominy and enjoyed warm or cool with meals.
ingredients: 1/2 tsp baking soda (to stand in for traditional wood-ash lye)
steps: Rinse the grits in a strainer.
Bring the water to a boil in a large pot and stir in the grits, baking soda, and salt.
Reduce the heat to low and simmer, stirring occasionally, for 1 1/2 hours, adding water as needed to keep it thin and drinkable.
The corn should be very soft and the liquid creamy and pourable.
Serve warm, or let stand at room temperature for a day to develop the traditional slightly sour flavor, then refrigerate.

original.title: Haudenosaunee Strawberry Drink
original.description: A sweet, crushed strawberry drink served at the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Strawberry Festival, giving thanks for the first fruit of the year.
steps: Crush the strawberries in a large bowl with a potato masher until juicy but still a little chunky.
Stir in the maple syrup and let stand for 15 minutes.
Add the cold water and stir well.
Taste and add more maple syrup if needed.
Chill and serve over ice with some of the crushed berries in each glass.

original.title: Maple Roasted Sunchokes
original.description: Sunchokes (Jerusalem artichokes), a native tuber cultivated by Eastern tribes, roasted with sage and maple until crisp outside and creamy inside.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb sunchokes, scrubbed and cut into 1-inch pieces
steps: Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
Toss the sunchokes with the oil, maple syrup, sage, salt, and pepper.
Spread in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet.
Roast for 30–35 minutes, turning once, until browned and tender when pierced.
Serve hot.

original.title: Cherokee Ramps and Eggs
original.description: Wild ramps fried with potatoes and scrambled eggs, a springtime breakfast tradition among the Eastern Band of Cherokee in the Smoky Mountains.
steps: Separate the ramp leaves from the white bulbs and stems and chop each separately.
Heat the bacon fat in a large skillet over medium heat.
Add the potatoes and salt and fry for 10–12 minutes, turning, until tender and golden.
Add the chopped ramp bulbs and cook for 2 minutes.
Stir in the ramp leaves and cook 1 minute until wilted.
Pour in the eggs and gently scramble with the vegetables until just set.
Season with pepper and serve hot.
